title: Playing high schools and colleges; Kenton's push to teach
summary: Nearly 80 percent of recent dates were in schools and colleges; Stan Kenton persuaded him to do clinics in the 1970s.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Marvelous. Well, why don't we zero in a little bit on your contributions there, and back and forth? Because in a sense, you're paying back, if you want to use that word, to education what you've been really getting from them, and it's a product in dividends, too.
Well, yes, and I think that this past year and the year before, it's reaching a point that I'm most pleased about. If other things went as well, I would be com-

pletely intrigued, and that is simply the fact that this past year, almost 80 percent of all of our dates were in high schools and colleges, and that to me is a very healthy scene. That's where I'd rather be, either as a parttime educator or as just a person who comes to play some music.
Either way, I enjoy it very much.
Well, you've been doing clinics and seminars for a long time.
Quite a few years now, but I think -- now we've finally reached the point where it's -- the majority of our time is spent there -- and that's when I'm happiest and I find the bands grooves the most.
I recall you were beginning with that --

And something that might also be of interest to people who are not aware that -- I was convinced more by Stan Kenton wanting to convince me to do it than by anyone else. He felt it would be part of my surviving a bad -- not a particularly bad period, but a period that was tough.
And he felt that this would be good therapy for me, plus the fact that it's a much sounder thing than doing things you really don't like to do.
